meta.note:
Built to the same shape as the writing corpus — FUNCTION is the unit and the browsing axis, categories group the carousel without gating it — with two changes that the spoken exam forces.

FIRST, THE AXIS IS NOT REGISTER. Writing grades phrases informal → neutral → formal. For a spoken bank aimed at teenagers that axis mislabels almost everything: 'Naturally' and 'No doubt' are not FORMAL, they are OLD. A fifteen-year-old saying them sounds like a coursebook, and an examiner hears exactly that. Meanwhile 'To be honest' is thoroughly informal and completely at home in a teenager's mouth. So the field is `mouth` — teen, adult, or both — and register is deliberately absent. The writing corpus's own rule applies: showing an axis that is not there would be a lie.

SECOND, SPEAKING NEEDS FUNCTIONS WRITING DOES NOT HAVE. Buying time is the clearest case. It is missing from all 45 writing functions because a student facing a blank page can take four minutes; a candidate in Part 4 has two seconds. The same goes for taking the floor back, repairing yourself mid-sentence, and asking for repetition.

`from` is provenance, checked by script, not claimed in a comment. 'turn' means the phrase appears in a model turn the student will actually meet in Parts 1 to 4. 'bank' means it was added for range and appears nowhere yet — honestly labelled rather than silently mixed in.
meta.mouthNote: teen — a fifteen-year-old can say this without flinching. adult — correct English, but it will sound borrowed in a teenager's mouth. both — no age signal either way. A card should show the teen/adult marker only where it discriminates; on a function where every phrase is `both`, showing it says nothing.
meta.conventionNote: The most valuable field in the writing corpus, and it matters more here: in speech there is no time to reconsider a phrase that has misfired. These are the notes that stop a phrase bank producing confident, fluent rudeness.
meta.shapeNote:
TWO SHAPES, and Part 2 proved it rather than my assuming it. A similarity phrase OPENS a sentence — 'Both photos show…' — while a difference phrase JOINS two halves of one: 'whereas', 'while', 'on the other hand' appear 32 times between them in the model turns, always mid-sentence. `joins: true` marks the second kind.

This matters more in speech than in writing. A student who has only ever seen 'whereas' in a list will try to begin a sentence with it, and in a spoken exam there is no chance to go back and fix it. The bank has to show which phrases can start a sentence and which cannot.

fluency.label: Keeping going
fluency.note: Buying time, holding the floor, repairing yourself. The real-time half of speaking, and absent from writing entirely.

stance.label: Stance and attitude
stance.note: Reacting, agreeing, conceding. Shared with the writing corpus, different mouths.

interaction.label: With your partner
interaction.note: Parts 3 and 4, where Interactive Communication is marked.

describing.label: Describing and comparing
describing.note: Part 2's long turn. Openers for what is shared, joiners for what differs.

buying_time.label: Buying time
buying_time.when: to take a moment without going silent
buying_time.criterion: Discourse Management — a filled pause is fluent; an empty one is hesitation.

phrases.note: The workhorse. Almost invisible, which is the point.
Signals you are about to start, not that you are stuck.
Longer than 'Honestly' — buys roughly a second more.
Says out loud that you are thinking. Use once, not twice.
Common, and examiners hear it constantly. Safer in Part 4 than Part 1.
Also repairs: it can introduce a second attempt at the same idea.
Careful: it signals a correction. See the convention note.
Sets up an explanation. In a teenager's mouth it can sound like lecturing.
Buys time AND is a real answer — the best of both.
For when the exact word will not come.
Buys the most time of anything here, and draws the most attention to itself.

buying_time.convention:
A filled pause is fluent English; an empty one is hesitation, and Discourse Management scores them differently. Portuguese learners often go silent while searching for a word, which reads as a gap rather than as thinking.

'Actually' is the trap. In English it CONTRADICTS something — a fact, an expectation, what the other person just said. Used as a filler it contradicts things nobody said, and it can sound combative. Portuguese 'na verdade' is far milder.

One filler per turn. Two in a row is the hesitation the filler was meant to hide.

misfires.t: Actually, I usually see my friends.
misfires.why: Nobody suggested otherwise. 'Actually' has nothing to contradict, so it just sounds argumentative.
Four fillers is not thinking time, it is panic. The examiner hears the panic, not the phrases.
On a Part 1 question like 'Do you live in a house or a flat?' this is absurd. Keep it for Part 4.

reacting.label: Reacting
reacting.when: to show how you feel before you answer
reacting.criterion: Discourse Management — a reaction is the clearest way to organise an answer, and it buys two seconds.

phrases.note: Slightly theatrical, which teenagers can carry and adults often cannot.
Two markers at once. Natural in speech, almost never written.
The missing register: a teenager who dislikes the topic needs this.

phrases.t: I can't say I'm keen on …
I've never been that bothered about …

phrases.note: Careful — see the convention note.
Correct English. In a teenager's mouth it sounds borrowed.
Same. Appears nowhere in the model turns for a reason.
A pseudo-cleft: marks the discourse AND counts as a complex structure.

phrases.t: The thing I love about … is …
If there's one thing I …, it's …

reacting.convention:
'Of course' can sound impatient in English — close to 'obviously you should know that' — where Portuguese 'claro' is neutral. Agreeing with a partner with 'Of course' or 'Naturally' can read as condescending.

The clefts earn twice: they mark the discourse for Discourse Management and count as complex structures for Grammatical Resource. One phrase, two criteria.

Every model answer in Part 1 is enthusiastic. Real candidates are not. A student who finds the topic dull needs 'I'm not really into…' more than another way to say 'I love'.

misfires.t: Naturally, I spend most of it with my friends.
misfires.why: Nothing about it is natural or obvious to the examiner. The word claims a shared assumption that isn't there.

misfires.t: Of course I like my hometown.
misfires.why: Reads as 'why would you even ask'. In Portuguese 'claro' would be fine here; in English it is faintly rude.

partly_agreeing.label: Agreeing, but only so far
partly_agreeing.when: to accept your partner's point and keep your own
partly_agreeing.criterion: Interactive Communication — the single most useful move in Part 3.

phrases.t: Yeah, I see what you mean.

phrases.note: The commonest real version, and perfectly acceptable at B2.

phrases.t: That's one way of looking at it.
I'd agree up to a point.

partly_agreeing.convention:
English disagreement is hedged far more than Portuguese. Leading with a concession and then turning is the default, not a politeness flourish — a bare 'No, because…' reads as blunt even when the reasoning is good.

Every one of these must be followed by something of your own. The concession alone ends the exchange and hands your partner all the work, which is exactly what Interactive Communication marks down.

'I couldn't agree more' is STRONG AGREEMENT, not disagreement. The negative form misleads learners constantly.

comparing.label: What they share
comparing.when: to open the long turn with what the two photographs have in common
comparing.criterion: Discourse Management — Part 2 is a comparison, not two descriptions. Opening here is what makes it one.

phrases.t: In both photographs we can see …
In both pictures we can see …
What they have in common is …
One thing both situations have in common is …
Both of them seem to be …

comparing.convention:
Describing photo one and then photo two is the commonest way to lose Part 2. It is two descriptions, not a comparison, and Discourse Management marks the difference. Opening with what they SHARE forces the turn into a comparison from the first sentence.

'Both' takes a plural verb: both photos SHOW, not shows. It is also a Use of English item, so it is worth getting right twice over.

misfires.t: In the first photo, there is a man in an office.
misfires.why: A description, not a comparison. Nothing has been compared yet, and the minute has started.
'Both' is plural: both photos show. A small slip, and an examiner hears it immediately.

contrasting.label: How they differ
contrasting.when: to turn the description into a comparison
contrasting.criterion: Discourse Management, and Grammatical Resource — these are subordinating structures, not just linkers.

phrases.note: The commonest in the model turns by far — 16 uses.
Can also open a sentence, unlike the two above.
Opens a sentence. The one contrast phrase here that can.

phrases.t: But there are some big differences …

contrasting.convention:
'Whereas' and 'while' JOIN two halves of one sentence. They cannot start a sentence on their own, and a student who has only met them in a list will try. In writing that gets corrected on the second draft; in a spoken exam it is simply heard.

'However' is the opposite: it opens a sentence and is followed by a comma. Learners regularly swap the two.

One contrast is enough in a sixty-second turn. Two is description dressed up as comparison, and it eats the time the question needs.

misfires.t: Whereas the second photo shows a café.
misfires.why: A fragment. 'Whereas' needs a first half to attach to — the sentence has no main clause.
'However' takes a comma: However, they are different. Without it, it reads as 'in whatever way'.

speculating.label: Guessing about people
speculating.when: to answer the question about people you have never met
speculating.criterion: Grammatical Resource — modal verbs are the structure this whole move is built on.

phrases.note: The commonest in the model turns — 11 uses.
Informal and very natural for a teenager. Fine at B2.
Correct, and it will sound borrowed at fifteen.

speculating.convention:
You are guessing about strangers in a photograph, and you should sound like it. A candidate who says 'They are bored' is claiming to know something they cannot; 'They might be bored' is the same observation, correctly hedged, and it uses a modal — which is what Grammatical Resource is looking for here.

Portuguese learners often state the guess flatly, because the hedging is carried by intonation in Portuguese and by the verb in English.

misfires.t: They are finding it difficult to concentrate.
misfires.why: You cannot know that. The observation is fine; the certainty is not, and it throws away the modal the examiner is listening for.
One hedge per guess. Doubling it sounds unsure of the language rather than of the answer.

managing_minute.label: Getting to the question
managing_minute.when: to move from describing to answering before the minute runs out
managing_minute.criterion: Discourse Management — Part 2 is half description, half answer. The move between them is the whole task.

phrases.t: As for what might be difficult, …

managing_minute.convention:
Every model turn in this app runs 57 to 65 seconds against a 60-second limit, and the question is always the longest of the three parts. A candidate who describes until the interlocutor stops them has answered nothing, and the question is where the marks are.

These phrases are the hinge. Saying one out loud commits you to the second half of the task, which is exactly their value: they are as much a cue to yourself as a signal to the examiner.

Aim to reach one of these by about thirty seconds.

misfires.why: The commonest way to lose Part 2. Everything said was correct and the question was never answered.
